Looky Model Benchmark

2026-11-02Looky 1c806ba + reasoning-effort patchpaws-app 2ac9302310 pilot questions × Fast and Deep

Real models answered the ten paws-app pilot questions through Looky's MCP endpoint and its React app. Every answer below is the model's own text, scored by hand against the pilot's reviewer key and checked against the pinned commit.

Recommendation

Fast defaultminimax-m3.1-flash, effort low

OpenCode Go. 8/10 useful, median 5.1 s, 10 calls with no repairs and no truncation. Cheapest answer per question.

Deep defaultminimax-m3.1-flash, effort low

9/10 useful, median 36 s. Ties the others on quality and stays on the Go plan. Looky picks one provider per session, so one model serves both modes today.

If Deep latency mattersgemini-3.8-flash, effort low

OpenRouter. Same 8/10 and 9/10, Deep median 22 s, but about 5× the cost per Deep answer and it labels too many answers "supported".

All three full-run models clear the 8/10 bar in Deep. In Fast, MiniMax and Gemini reach 8/10 and GLM 5.3 Flash reaches 6/10. No answer cited a range outside its revision or invented evidence. MiniMax only works with the new REASONING_EFFORT=low setting; without it the model returns empty replies.

q08 (stale documentation) failed for every model in both modes. Deep never retrieved the [queue] and [caps] branches of assignConfig that silently ignore unknown keys, so no model could see that the docs overstate the check. That is a retrieval gap, not a model choice.

What the benchmark found in Looky

  • High · fixed on branchReasoning models spend the whole output budget before answering

    DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MiniMax M3.1 Flash and Haiku 5.5 returned empty or truncated replies: reasoning tokens equalled max_tokens (1,500 in Fast, 600 for a Deep plan). Looky had no way to ask for less reasoning. The new optional LOOKY_PROVIDER_<ID>_REASONING_EFFORT sends reasoning_effort on the OpenAI-compatible kind and turns MiniMax from 0/2 to a clean pass.

  • MediumFast synthesis leaves no room for its own JSON repair

    Fast gives the synthesis call the whole output budget, so when that reply is truncated the repair call has nothing left (GLM q05, Haiku, Gemini Flash-Lite). Reserving part of the budget, or capping synthesis below it, would let the repair run.

  • MediumFast retrieval bounds Fast quality

    Model-free Fast research hits 11 of 29 pinned ranges and Deep 16 of 29. Fast q06 found only docs for every model, and q01 Fast quality varied with how much a model could infer from five ranges.

  • LowUnparsed citation markers leak into prose

    Markers such as [E1:56,85] and [E2:5,36,79-81], with comma-separated lines, are neither linked nor removed.

  • LowRationale guard fires on questions that ask no "why"

    "The answer described a reason that no cited documentation states" and a generic question for the team appear on q02 and q03, which ask what happens, not why.

  • LowCaveats are cut at 400 characters mid-sentence; backticks show raw in the UI

    One GLM caveat ends in "looks counterintuitive; the". Caveat text renders `code` literally in the React app.

  • LowOne provider serves both modes

    A session selects one provider policy, so Fast and Deep cannot use different models without two configured providers and client-side routing.

React app with real answers

The built app was served on 127.0.0.1 with local auth and driven in headless Chromium against MiniMax M3.1 Flash at low effort. The page pinned 2ac93023d31bab6f0ef26690a7e6e8e8d2540bff (equal to the clone's HEAD) and reported the index ready after 0.0 s. For each answer the first three source links were checked to name the pinned SHA and lines that exist in the file. Spend

OpenCode Go

162 requests including probes and the UI run. Estimated $0.31 at catalogue list prices, with DeepSeek's peak-hour multiplier applied. Go did not report opencode.allowance on any response, so the plan allowance used is not measured. Hard cap $3.00 / 500 requests was never reached.

OpenRouter

79 requests. $0.62 from the cost OpenRouter reports per response; the key's own usage counter read $0.62 of its $3.00 limit afterwards. Proxy cap $2.80 was never reached.

Every answer

q01fastMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful7.0 sWhat does Paws do with work items that were in flight when the process starts up again?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Resume/reattach/reverify, merge queue with GitHub check, skips, ask-restart. Misses the 5 s stagger.

Paws recovers interrupted work items during startup rather than restarting everything from scratch. Running or verifying work is resumed in a fresh session from its checkpoint—or from its branch if no checkpoint exists—and, when the runner still holds the work, Paws reattaches to the existing command; a verifying item is instead re-verified. (src/core/recovery.ts:75-105)

Items in the merge queue keep their place. If a GitHub merge call may have been in flight when the process stopped, Paws asks GitHub whether that call completed before moving the item forward, avoiding a duplicate merge. (src/core/recovery.ts:76-82) (src/db/remote-merges.ts:78-80) Work that already has a pending capacity wait, answer resume, or transient retry is left alone, while an item that was already resumed once may trigger a Linear question asking whether it should be started again. (src/db/recovery.ts:57-74) (src/db/recovery.ts:103-113)

In broad terms, the deployment documentation says runners continue working while Paws is down and Paws reattaches to the same commands after startup, including in-flight Closeout reviews and answer tasks. (README.md:52-55)

This is based on 5 source ranges in 5 files, not the whole repository. Asking again with mode "deep" can follow the remaining leads.

Caveats
  • The inspected evidence does not include the implementations of `applyDecision`, the individual queue handlers, or the exact GitHub reconciliation path.
  • The README references to `blocks`, `checks`, and `failedChecks` were not checked against implementation code.
  • README.md:1-75 mentions `blocks`, `checks`, `failedChecks`; Fast did not check these against code at this revision.
  • Based on 5 inspected source ranges in 5 files at commit 2ac93023d31b; the rest of the repository was not read for this answer.
Expected (reviewer key)

recoverOnStartup runs in one immediate transaction: it shifts runner leases for downtime, lists items in awaiting_input, running, verifying, recovering and merge_queue, skips items that already have a restart question, a parked capacity wait, a pending answer resume or a pending transient retry, and asks decideStartup what to do. decideStartup returns none for non-resumable states, keep_place for a merge-queue item whose run is not active, reverify when a merge was in progress or the runner still holds a verifying item, resume with reattach when the runner holds work, ask_restart when the item was already resumed within RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS, reverify for a verifying item with a candidate, and otherwise a fresh-session resume from the checkpoint. Resumes are staggered five seconds apart.

q01deepMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful24.5 sWhat does Paws do with work items that were in flight when the process starts up again?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome partial

Review: All branches plus 5 s spacing; awaiting_input described as parked (also releases capacity and enqueues a catch-up job). One citation removed by Looky.

Paws does not blindly restart everything that was in flight. On startup, recoverOnStartup examines items in awaiting_input, running, verifying, recovering, and merge_queue, then chooses a recovery action for each. (src/db/recovery.ts:31-39) (src/db/recovery.ts:51-74)

- Running or verifying work: If a runner still holds the item’s work, Paws resumes it in a fresh session, using the saved checkpoint when available, and reattaches to the existing runner command. A verifying item whose Closeout review or check run is still held by a runner instead re-verifies. (src/core/recovery.ts:94-105) This is consistent with the README’s statement that runners keep working while Paws is down and that Paws reattaches to the same commands after startup. (README.md:52-55)
- Merge-queue work: Paws keeps the item’s queue position. If a GitHub merge call may have been in flight, the merge job first checks GitHub before taking further action; a still-active run causes the item to re-verify instead. (src/core/recovery.ts:75-83) (src/core/recovery.ts:95-97) The durable merge_call row is what marks a merge call as potentially in flight. (src/db/remote-merges.ts:78-80)
- Interrupted verification or merge progress: If the checkpoint shows that merging had already begun, Paws re-verifies rather than treating the work as an ordinary implementation resume. (src/core/recovery.ts:97-98)
- Work already resumed recently: After a prior recovery attempt, a later restart within the configured interval asks in Linear whether to start the item again rather than automatically resuming it. A sufficiently old prior resume is automatically resumed again. (src/core/recovery.ts:101-105) (src/core/recovery.test.ts:82-108)
- Open questions: An item awaiting input remains parked; startup does not create a resume job. The answer later resumes the original run, and the test confirms the item stays awaiting_input with no new resume job during recovery. (test/loop.question-resume.test.ts:156-180)
- Already-scheduled follow-up work: Capacity waits and pending answer resumes or transient retries are left alone because their next attempt is already queued. (src/db/recovery.ts:62-64) (src/db/recovery.ts:103-113)

The recovery pass runs inside one transaction, and applyDecision dispatches each decision to its corresponding persistence and follow-up operation. Resume work is scheduled with five-second spacing rather than all being started simultaneously. (src/db/recovery.ts:75-87) (src/db/decisions.ts:17-26) The README summarizes the intended operational behavior as: a restart is safe during running work, runners retain their results, and Paws reattaches after startup, including in-flight Closeout reviews and answer tasks. (README.md:52-55)

q02fastMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful6.6 sWhat happens when Paws restarts again while a task it already resumed once after a restart is still unfinished?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Rule and precedence correct; window value marked unseen.

Paws does not automatically resume that task a second time. On the next startup, if its recovery attempt count is already at least one and less than RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS has elapsed since the previous resume, Paws returns an ask_restart decision and asks in Linear whether to start it again. The task therefore remains unfinished pending that answer. (src/core/recovery.ts:101-105) (src/db/recovery.ts:57-60)

There are higher-priority exceptions. There are exceptions to this normal ask_restart result. On SIGTERM, Paws starts its normal shutdown path with exit code 0; the signal handler calls shutdownPaws, while the recovery shutdown routine first commits a WIP snapshot for each in-flight item. q03deepMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful61.0 sWhat does Paws do to running work items when it shuts down on SIGTERM?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Complete incl. commit policy, merge queue and exit codes.

On SIGTERM, Paws invokes the normal shutdown path: the signal handler calls shutdownPaws, which awaits paws.stop() and then exits. The stop routine first stops the running components, then performs a durable state flush through prepareShutdown, and finally closes the database. Shutdown failures are journaled; a failure in the state flush or database close can result in exit code 1. (src/index.ts:2054-2062) (src/shutdown.ts:60-77) (src/index.ts:1544-1583)

During the flush, Paws attempts to commit a WIP checkpoint for each in-flight item. The callback performs a synchronous commit in the item's worktree with the message wip: shutdown when the item has a stored commit policy. If one commit fails, Paws journals the error and continues; the work-item lease/state transition still proceeds, so a missing worktree does not prevent shutdown. (src/index.ts:1567-1577) (src/db/recovery.ts:178-187) (src/db/recovery.ts:28-29)

prepareShutdown then marks Paws alive and examines items in the running and verifying states. An item is left unchanged if it is parked waiting for capacity or if a runner still holds its work. The latter can include an active agent turn or a verification closeout/check run. Otherwise, Paws marks the item's current run as lost and, except for verification items whose verification state is preserved, applies a lease_expired event. The implementation comment describes this as moving running work to recovering without using the one resume attempt, while retaining state for work still held by a runner. (src/db/recovery.ts:165-171) (src/db/recovery.ts:188-195) (src/db/recovery.ts:208-214)

Merge-queue items are handled separately. If the associated run is still active, Paws marks that run lost and applies lease_expired; merge-queue items without an active run are left in place. The implementation comment states that waiting merge-queue items retain their state and their place in the queue for the next startup, while an item whose run is still active is left for re-verification. (src/db/recovery.ts:196-200) (src/db/recovery.ts:204-205)

The shutdown test verifies that SIGTERM exits with code 0, creates the wip: shutdown commit, and leaves the affected item in recovering. The same test separately confirms that an unrelated queued item remains queued. (test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:249-262) (test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:196-215)

q04fastMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful5.1 sHow does a Linear webhook delivery become work for the orchestrator?
2/2 correct1/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Handler pipeline right; says route and downstream not shown.

A Linear webhook becomes orchestrator work through handleLinearWebhook: the handler authenticates and validates the delivery, durably commits it to the InboxStore, then dispatches it through either the IntakeQueue or the onEvent callback. The intent is to acknowledge Linear quickly: the HTTP 200 is returned after commit, while follow-up work is handed to a queue worker or scheduled asynchronously. (src/linear/webhook.ts:102-106) (src/linear/webhook.ts:145-152)

The conversion begins by requiring a Linear signature and secret, checking that the signature is hexadecimal, reading at most 1 MiB of raw request data, verifying its HMAC-SHA256, checking that the timestamp is within 60 seconds, requiring a delivery ID, and parsing the body into an AcceptedLinearEvent. Invalid signatures, stale timestamps, malformed payloads, or missing delivery IDs are rejected; a missing persisted store produces a 500 because the event cannot be safely accepted. (src/linear/webhook.ts:63-72) (src/linear/webhook.ts:107-144) (src/linear/webhook.ts:177-180) Parsing extracts the agent-session and activity fields, maps the Linear type/action to an internal action such as created, prompted, or another accepted action, determines stop signals, and computes a deduplication key. (src/linear/webhook.ts:198-254)

After successful validation, the handler records the verified-delivery cursor, clears verification-failure tracking, and commits the event to the inbox for deduplication and persistence. For events accepted by IntakeQueue—documented as created and prompted—a newly inserted event is sent with intake.arrive, while a previously seen but unhandled event only wakes the queue. The queue’s worker then performs the first activity and intake work. Otherwise, schedule invokes deps.onEvent(event), which is the webhook-to-orchestrator callback path; after it resolves, the event is marked handled. The callback is deliberately not awaited before the webhook response. (src/linear/webhook.ts:39-45) (src/linear/webhook.ts:103-105) (src/linear/webhook.ts:145-152) (src/linear/webhook.ts:155-170)

Delivery IDs and deduplication prevent the same webhook from becoming repeated work. schedule also maintains an in-flight deduplication set so concurrent callbacks for the same dedupeKey are not launched simultaneously, and callback failures are journaled rather than being propagated into the already-successful HTTP acknowledgement. (src/linear/webhook.ts:147-152) (src/linear/webhook.ts:155-170)

Review: Route, verification, intake (2, retry ladder), schedule; does not reach onLinearEvent and says so.

A Linear webhook becomes orchestrator work through a two-stage path: the HTTP delivery is authenticated, normalized, and committed to the Linear inbox, then the event is offered to either the intake queue or an asynchronous onEvent callback. The inspected evidence establishes that dispatch boundary, but it does not show the callback, intake worker, or the code that finally creates an orchestrator work item, so that last transition cannot be traced fully. (src/linear/webhook.ts:102-170) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:21-34)

The server exposes POST /webhooks/linear and routes it to handleLinearWebhook(request, secrets.linearWebhookSecret, secrets.linearWebhook) when webhook support is enabled. The configured Linear runtime’s webhook dependency is preferred, with an inbox-only fallback. (src/server/serve.ts:664-673) (src/index.ts:964-974)

handleLinearWebhook performs this sequence:

1. It requires a linear-signature header and configured secret, checks that the signature is a 64-character hexadecimal value, and reads the raw body with a 1 MiB limit. readWebhookBody also limits concurrent readers, enforces a timeout, and can return 400, 408, 413, or 503 for invalid, timed-out, oversized, or overloaded intake. (src/linear/webhook.ts:112-130) (src/webhook-body/index.ts:4-45)

2. It verifies an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw body and then checks the timestamp against the 60-second window. The timestamp comes from the JSON body’s webhookTimestamp, falling back to the linear-timestamp header. It also requires a nonempty linear-delivery ID. (src/linear/webhook.ts:17-36) (src/linear/webhook.ts:126-140) (src/linear/webhook.ts:182-196)

3. parseAgentEvent parses and normalizes the payload into an AcceptedLinearEvent, extracting the action, session and issue IDs, activity ID, prompt body and signal, calculating a deduplication key, and retaining the raw payload. A closed Linear session is represented as a prompted event with a stop signal, as is a prompt body beginning with /paws stop. (src/linear/webhook.ts:198-254) (src/linear/event-dispatch.ts:14-16)

4. A persistent inbox store is required. After accepting the event, the handler updates the linear:webhook verification cursor, clears the in-memory verification-failure count, and calls store.commit(event). The commit result tells the handler whether the event was newly inserted and whether it had already been handled. (src/linear/webhook.ts:142-152) (src/linear/inbox.ts:5-32)

5. created and prompted events, except stops, go through the IntakeQueue. A newly inserted event is passed to intake.arrive(event); an already-recorded but unhandled event causes intake.wake(). The queue’s documented behavior is to post the first Linear activity immediately and then let its worker take the event. Intake supports two concurrent operations, and its documented retry schedule is 30 seconds, 60 seconds, 2 minutes, 5 minutes, and then 10 minutes. (src/linear/webhook.ts:147-151) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:9-34)

6. Other events, including immediate stops, use schedule. If onEvent is configured, the handler records the deduplication key in an in-memory pending set and invokes the callback asynchronously. On success it marks the event handled in the inbox; on failure it journals the error. The handler does not await that follow-up, allowing the acknowledgement to remain within Linear’s five-second budget. The acknowledgement test exercises this with both the Linear follow-up and Linear HTTP client deliberately stalled. (src/linear/webhook.ts:102-105) (src/linear/webhook.ts:151-170) (test/linear-webhook-ack.test.ts:63-98)

After a successful verification, parse, and commit, the handler returns a JSON acknowledgement indicating whether the delivery was a duplicate. A duplicate that is already handled is acknowledged without being dispatched again. Missing or bad signatures, a missing secret, a bad HMAC, a stale or missing timestamp, and a missing delivery ID are rejected; bad_payload is rejected with 400, while the other reasons handled by reject use 401. If no inbox store is configured, the handler returns 500 with reason not_persisted. (src/linear/webhook.ts:139-152) (src/linear/webhook.ts:177-180)

The inspected evidence therefore supports the transition from a verified webhook to a committed, normalized inbox event and then to either queue intake or callback dispatch. It does not expose the body of onEvent, the IntakeQueue worker, or the code that converts an accepted event into an orchestrator work item, so the exact final orchestrator call and work-item creation mechanism remain unestablished. (src/linear/runtime.ts:34-50)

q05fastMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful8.9 sHow does a person's bypass of a failed Closeout check reach the Closeout decision?
2/2 correct1/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: applyBypasses rules and outcome; says the adapter from DB rows to gate input is not shown.

A person’s bypass is applied during evaluation by applyBypasses. It accepts an approval only when it matches the decision’s task, base commit, head commit, and policy digest; it must also have a nonempty actor and reason and identify one or more check IDs present in the decision. Each referenced check may be failed, exhausted, independence, passed, or skipped (src/closeout/bypass.ts:21-43). The closeout gate accepts bypass approvals through its bypasses option and uses decide to decide from the evidence already recorded for a head, without rerunning commands or review (src/closeout/gate.ts:30-37) (src/closeout/gate.ts:40-60).

For a matching approval, applyBypasses removes the bypassed check IDs from the items that still require a successful outcome. It then recomputes the Closeout outcome: if nothing remains, the decision is accepted; if any remaining item is exhausted, it is exhausted; if every remaining item is failed, it is rejected; otherwise it is blocked. The applied approvals are returned with the evaluation (src/closeout/bypass.ts:44-60). A skipped item whose message is setup failed is not removed by the bypass filter, so it remains relevant unless its check ID is explicitly bypassed (src/closeout/bypass.ts:45-50).

The database layer preserves the offered failed check, the person’s reason and name, and the approving Linear user ID and timestamp. These records are read back with the original check state and message when the item page is loaded (src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:3-20) (src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:57-74).

A bypass is approved on the item page, not by a Linear reply. recoveryOptions reads the item's Closeout recoveries and, for link asks decided 'approve', turns each approved check with a reason into a CloseoutBypass carrying task, base, head and policy digest. The orchestrator spreads recoveryOptions into the Closeout gate options, and evaluateCandidate applies applyBypasses to the native evaluation. A bypass only counts when task, base, head and policy digest match exactly and the check is bypassable; the outcome becomes accepted only when nothing else remains, and the summary lists who approved each bypass.

q05deepMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful38.9 sHow does a person's bypass of a failed Closeout check reach the Closeout decision?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Full path incl. recoveryOptions, item-page approval, Linear reply is only guidance, docs binding.

A person’s bypass reaches the Closeout decision as a CloseoutBypass approval: it is loaded from the persisted bypass-check rows, supplied through GateInput.bypasses, and applied by applyBypasses after Closeout has formed an evaluation. The approved check is removed from the unsatisfied items; if nothing unsatisfied remains, the evaluation outcome becomes accepted.(src/closeout/bypass.ts:21-60)(src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:14-53)(src/closeout/run.ts:497-532)

The flow is:

1. When Closeout stops with failed checks, askCloseoutHelp creates a link ask, records the recovery against that question, and saves the offered checks with saveCloseoutBypassChecks.(src/loop/closeout-help.ts:38-98) The saved check rows include fields for the reason, approver ID, approver name, and approval time.(src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:8-20)

2. When recovery options are prepared, recoveryOptions reads the closeout recoveries and their associated link asks. Only a link ask whose decision is approve contributes bypasses. For each saved check having both approvedBy and reason, it constructs a CloseoutBypass containing the recovery’s task, base, head, and policy digest, plus the check ID, actor, optional actor name, and reason.(src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:14-53) The inspected code does not include the database write that populates the approval fields, although the read path clearly expects them to have been stored there.(src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:57-74)(src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:38-51)

3. GateInput carries these approvals in its bypasses field, and the public CloseoutGateOptions exposes the same field to the gate implementation.(src/closeout/run.ts:89-116)(src/closeout/gate.ts:40-60)

4. In the recorded-decision path, decideCloseoutGate calls decideRecorded. After Closeout produces and normalizes the decision, decideRecorded passes input.bypasses?? [] to applyBypasses.(src/closeout/run.ts:474-495)(src/closeout/run.ts:497-532) This path decides from recorded evidence and does not run commands or the review again.(src/closeout/run.ts:469-484)

5. applyBypasses accepts an approval only when it matches the decision’s candidate task, base, head, and policy digest; its actor and reason are nonblank; and every named check exists in the decision. A named check may be in failed, exhausted, or independence state, or may already be passed or skipped.(src/closeout/bypass.ts:17-43) It then excludes the approved check IDs from the remaining unsatisfied items.(src/closeout/bypass.ts:44-51)

6. The resulting outcome is derived from those remaining items: none means accepted; any remaining exhausted item means exhausted; if all remaining items are failed, it means rejected; otherwise it means blocked.(src/closeout/bypass.ts:52-60) At the gate level, decideCloseoutGate converts a recorded rejected evaluation into exhausted before returning the final GateResult.(src/closeout/run.ts:493-495)

The documentation describes the intended binding in the same terms: a bypass is tied to the task, base, head, and policy digest, and the same head is verified again with the approval; a new commit causes checks to run again.(docs/closeout.md:162-168) A Linear reply such as /paws bypass... is only guidance and does not itself create an effective bypass; authorization must come from the item-page decision.(src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:20-27)(docs/closeout.md:162-168)

The queue start timeout is configured under the [queue] section of ~/.paws/config.toml as start_timeout_hours. Its default is 24 hours, and the documented accepted range is 1 to 720 hours (docs/configuration.md:36) (docs/configuration.md:79-82). The Settings page exposes the same setting as the queue-start-timeout field and converts its input into queue.startTimeoutHours when building the update request (src/web/src/client/agent-settings.ts:234-240). Validation requires a whole number from 1 through 720; invalid values—including 0, 721, 1.5, and NaN—produce the error “Queue start timeout: enter a whole number of hours from 1 to 720.” (src/web/src/client/agent-settings.test.ts:92-97). The configuration reference also states that an unknown key or a value Paws no longer accepts prevents startup and reports the relevant configuration line (docs/configuration.md:3-6).

It is [queue] start_timeout_hours in ~/.paws/config.toml. The parser accepts any non-negative integer; readQueueSettings defaults a missing value to 24 hours and clamps it to 1..720. The queue start timeout is configured as start_timeout_hours in the [queue] section of ~/.paws/config.toml, for example:

[queue]

The configuration reference identifies the [queue] section and start_timeout_hours key, and the TOML loader stores it as PawsConfigFile.queueStartTimeoutHours. (docs/configuration.md:22-36) (src/config/file.ts:109-116) (src/config/file.ts:550-553) It can also be changed through the Settings UI: the browser reads the queue-start-timeout field into queue.startTimeoutHours, and the settings handler passes the submitted queue settings through parseQueueSettings before writing the configuration. (src/web/src/client/agent-settings.ts:229-240) (src/settings/handler.ts:104-127)

The default is 24 hours. It is the documented default, the value of DEFAULT_QUEUE_START_TIMEOUT_HOURS, the fallback used when the key is absent, the fallback used when the configuration cannot be read at dispatch time, and the value displayed by the UI when no timeout is configured. (docs/configuration.md:79-82) (src/config/queue.ts:3-4) (src/config/queue.ts:10-13) (src/web/src/client/agent-settings.test.ts:82-98) (src/loop/orchestrator.ts:4690-4704)

(src/config/queue.ts:43-53) (src/settings/handler.ts:104-117) The browser validation applies the same range and integer requirement, displaying Queue start timeout: enter a whole number of hours from 1 to 720. for values such as 0, 721, 1.5, or NaN. (src/web/src/client/agent-settings.test.ts:82-98)

A separately loaded TOML value follows a different path. The TOML assignment shown here parses start_timeout_hours as an integer, but this range is not checked in assignConfig. (src/config/file.ts:550-553) Later, readQueueSettings applies Math.min(Math.max(hours, 1), 720), so it supplies the 24-hour default when the value is missing and clamps the loaded number to the 1–720 range; it does not reject an out-of-range number there. (src/config/queue.ts:10-18) The orchestrator reads this setting on each dispatch. When the queued wait reaches hours * 3_600_000 milliseconds, it fails the item with reason start_timeout; if loading the configuration throws, it journals the error and uses the 24-hour default for that read. The queue-wait test covers the default behavior by showing that an item remains queued before one day and has failed with a message containing within 24 hours afterward. q07fastMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful14.5 sWhat happens when a Linear intake fails, and how is it retried?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: All paths and ladder; citations are coarse (whole 70-line ranges).

When a queued Linear intake fails, the queue catches the error, records it with store.markFailed, and leaves the event in the durable inbox for another attempt. The failure does not block unrelated queued events: each failed event waits on its own retry schedule, while the worker continues processing eligible events, subject to the configured concurrency of two. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-180)(src/linear/intake-queue.ts:36-107)

For ordinary failures, the queue increments the event's attempt count and schedules the next attempt using intakeRetryMs. The waits are 30 seconds, 60 seconds, 2 minutes, 5 minutes, and then 10 minutes for subsequent failures. pump skips events whose nextAttemptAt is still in the future and arms a timer for the earliest eligible retry; after delivery succeeds, the event is marked handled. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:1-35)(src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-180)(src/linear/intake-queue.ts:36-107)

There are two special cases. If the Linear session no longer exists, the event is logged and marked handled instead of being retried. If the failure is a LinearRateLimitError, the whole queue is paused until the rate limit expires, and the event is scheduled no earlier than the server's retryAfterMs (with a minimum of 30 seconds); this retry is not counted as a normal attempt. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-180)

The initial arrive activity is separate from the queued delivery. If that first activity fails, the error is journaled and logged, but the evidence shown does not mark the event handled or explicitly schedule a retry for it; the durable intake worker can still pick the event up through the inbox queue. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-180)(src/linear/intake-queue.ts:36-107)

This is based on 6 source ranges in 4 files, not the whole repository. Asking again with mode "deep" can follow the remaining leads.

Caveats
  • The evidence shows the queue and store interactions, but does not show the complete inbox-store implementation or the remainder of the retry test.
  • The exact behavior of a failure during the initial `arrive` phase after its logged error is not fully established by the shown code.
  • Based on 6 inspected source ranges in 4 files at commit 2ac93023d31b; the rest of the repository was not read for this answer.
Expected (reviewer key)

The intake worker catches the error and journals it. A missing AgentSession is marked handled and skipped. A Linear rate limit pauses the whole queue for its retry-after and reschedules the event without counting an attempt, waiting at least 30 seconds. Any other failure counts an attempt and reschedules that event after 30 s, 1 min, 2 min, 5 min, then every 10 min, without blocking other events, and logs the retry. Nothing is retried after the queue is stopped.

q07deepMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful27.1 sWhat happens when a Linear intake fails, and how is it retried?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome partial

Review: Matches the key incl. 'nothing retried after stop'. Two citations removed by Looky.

When queued Linear intake fails, the event remains in the durable inbox as unhandled. The queue records the error and schedules a later retry rather than immediately rerunning it; once delivery succeeds, the event is marked handled. A retry test confirms that failed intake remains unhandled with no work_item created, and that after closing and reopening SQLite the event is delivered again and disappears from the unhandled list after success. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-141) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:102-107)

For an ordinary failure, the queue increments the failed-attempt count, calculates a backoff, and calls store.markFailed with the error, nextAttemptAt, and counted: true. It then logs the attempt number and retry delay. The backoff sequence is 30 seconds, 1 minute, 2 minutes, 5 minutes, and 10 minutes; subsequent failures continue to use 10 minutes. A failed event has its own retry schedule and does not block other events, although events in the same session remain ordered. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:127-136) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:12-19) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:36-40)

The retry is driven by the queue’s pump function: queued events whose nextAttemptAt is still in the future are skipped, and the queue arms a timer for the earliest due retry. When that time arrives, the worker attempts the event again. The test observes exactly the six successive waits 30_000, 60_000, 120_000, 300_000, 600_000, and 600_000 milliseconds, while unrelated sessions continue to be delivered. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:73-100) (test/linear-intake-queue.test.ts:204-247)

Rate-limit failures use a different path. The queue pauses the entire queue until the maximum of the current hold and the error’s retryAfterMs, records the event as failed with counted: false, and schedules that event no earlier than the rate-limit delay. Because the attempt is not counted, it does not advance the ordinary backoff schedule. Even a zero-millisecond rate-limit response uses the minimum normal retry delay, preventing an immediate restart loop. A ledger-level hold also prevents any intake from starting and resumes the queue after the hold. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:118-125) (test/linear-intake-queue.test.ts:324-334)

There are two notable exceptions. If delivery reports that the Linear AgentSession no longer exists, the event is marked handled and skipped rather than retried. If the queue is stopped while handling an error, it exits without recording a retry. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-115)

The event’s initial “first activity” is separate from queued delivery. A failure in that arrival-phase activity is journaled and logged, after which the worker can handle the queued intake. For intake with no tracker configured, production delivery throws Linear is not connected, which is then handled by the queue’s ordinary failure-and-retry path. The production path passes the prior attempt count into delivery; failure reporting is enabled only for attempt zero, while the sessionBusy callback is passed separately to acknowledgeNewSession. (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:152-167) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:214-264)

The web status view exposes this state by showing the number of failed attempts, the time until the next retry, and the last error for each waiting intake. (src/web/src/client/intake.ts:37-46)

Review: Constant 5_000, scheduling not sleeping, rationale explicitly not established.

The inspected startup-recovery path does not sleep for five seconds between tasks; it schedules the resume jobs with staggered eligibility times. STARTUP_RESUME_SPACING_MS is set to 5_000, and recoverOnStartup assigns each applicable resume decision a runAt of now + STARTUP_RESUME_SPACING_MS * resumes++. Thus, the first scheduled resume is eligible at now, the next one five seconds later, and so on. (src/db/recovery.ts:31-40) (src/db/recovery.ts:53-57) (src/db/recovery.ts:83-86)

The decision and its follow-up work are persisted within the surrounding startup transaction. applyDecision receives the calculated runAt, and its resume branch passes that time into the resume path. (src/db/recovery.ts:51-57) (src/db/decisions.ts:17-32)

This spacing applies specifically to newly created resume work. Items that already have a parked capacity wait, pending answer resume, or pending transient retry are skipped, and a resume decision that can attach to an existing pending process_restart job does not create a replacement job. (src/db/recovery.ts:57-85) (src/db/recovery.ts:116-162) Other recovery outcomes also follow different paths: merge-queue work may keep its place, while verification-related work may re-verify rather than receive a resume with the five-second offset. (src/core/recovery.ts:56-61) (src/core/recovery.ts:75-105)

The inspected evidence does not state why this five-second spacing was introduced. It therefore does not establish whether the intent was to reduce a startup load spike, avoid contention, protect external services, or address some other concern. q10fastMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful3.3 sHow does Closeout decide a review finding's bug class, and when is a finding unclassified?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Both unclassified cases incl. 60 char limit.

Closeout derives a finding’s bug class from the beginning of its explanation. bugClass matches leading text up to the first :, em dash, - , period, semicolon, or newline, trims it, lowercases it, and returns that value. For example, "unchecked null: the handler reads …" becomes "unchecked null" (src/closeout/rounds.ts:21-28).

A finding is unclassified when that leading text is empty or when it is longer than the 60-character CLASS_LIMIT. In either case, bugClass returns the constant "unclassified" (src/closeout/rounds.ts:16-19) (src/closeout/rounds.ts:25-28). The resulting class is persisted with the finding as bug_class (src/db/review-findings.ts:164-180).

q10deepMiniMax M3.1 Flashuseful44.3 sHow does Closeout decide a review finding's bug class, and when is a finding unclassified?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Matches the key fully incl. tie-break.

Closeout derives a finding’s bug class solely from the start of its explanation, not from its severity or location. bugClass(explanation) extracts the leading text up to the first supported delimiter—a colon, em dash, " - ", period, semicolon, or newline—then trims and lowercases it. For example, "unchecked null: the handler reads …" becomes "unchecked null". (src/closeout/rounds.ts:21-29)

A finding is unclassified when the regex cannot extract a leading segment, when the extracted segment is empty, or when the trimmed segment is longer than 60 characters. In each case, bugClass returns the literal "unclassified". (src/closeout/rounds.ts:16-19) (src/closeout/rounds.ts:25-28) An unclassified finding remains labeled "unclassified" when it appears among the open findings in the review-round summary. (src/closeout/rounds.ts:69-80)

The classification is used in two related flows. When accepted review findings are recorded, each non-blocking finding’s explanation is passed through bugClass, and the result is stored in the database’s bug_class column. (src/loop/review-findings.ts:109-117) (src/db/review-findings.ts:162-179) Separately, summarizeReviewRounds classifies findings across review rounds. It excludes unclassified findings when determining the most frequent class, but still includes them in the displayed open findings with the "unclassified" label. If there are no classified findings, the summary’s overall bugClass is null; when class counts tie, the class from the later round wins. (src/closeout/rounds.ts:56-80)

q01fastGemini 3.8 Flashuseful11.1 sWhat does Paws do with work items that were in flight when the process starts up again?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Every decideStartup branch, skips, lease shift, stagger and awaiting_input handling, from 5 ranges. Best Fast q01 of the three.

When the Paws process starts up, recoverOnStartup inspects existing in-flight work items to decide whether to resume them, re-verify them, keep their queue position, or ask the user whether to restart (src/db/recovery.ts:46-54, src/core/recovery.ts:75-83). Before evaluating items, Paws shifts runner leases by the downtime duration (up to offlineBudgetMs) so outages do not penalize leases (src/db/recovery.ts:44, src/db/recovery.ts:52).

For each item in a startup state, Paws evaluates several conditions and computes a startup decision via decideStartup (src/db/recovery.ts:53-74, src/core/recovery.ts:84-92):

1. If an explicit restart question needs to be prompted (ensureRestartQuestion), or if an item has already exhausted its initial recovery attempt (recoveryAttempts >= 1) within the resume threshold without a runner holding the work, Paws outputs an ask_restart decision (src/db/recovery.ts:58-60, src/core/recovery.ts:101-102).
2. Items that have a parked capacity wait (hasParkedCapacityWait), a pending answer resume (hasPendingAnswerResume), or a pending transient retry (hasPendingTransientRetry) are skipped without scheduling redundant jobs (src/db/recovery.ts:62-64, src/db/recovery.ts:103-113).
3. Items waiting in the merge_queue keep their spot (keep_place) unless their run was still active, and track whether a merge call was in flight against GitHub (mergeCallInFlight) (src/db/recovery.ts:71, src/core/recovery.ts:95-96, src/db/remote-merges.ts:78-80).
4. If an item was mid-merge, if a run was cut short while active, or if it was in the verifying state while a runner still holds its work (or has a verification candidate), it transitions to reverify (src/core/recovery.ts:80-82, src/core/recovery.ts:94-98, src/core/recovery.ts:103-104).
5. Otherwise, resumable items are scheduled to resume in a fresh session from their checkpoint (or branch), reattaching if the runner still holds the work (src/core/recovery.ts:76-77, src/core/recovery.ts:99-100, src/core/recovery.ts:105).

Resume jobs are spaced apart using STARTUP_RESUME_SPACING_MS (src/db/recovery.ts:55-56, src/db/recovery.ts:85). Finally, any items in the awaiting_input state release their run capacity, and a catch-up job is enqueued if open questions remain (src/db/recovery.ts:89-98).

q01deepGemini 3.8 Flashuseful20.9 sWhat does Paws do with work items that were in flight when the process starts up again?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Complete and well structured; 5 s stagger with the constant.

When the process starts up again, Paws runs recoverOnStartup within an immediate database transaction to evaluate all work items in active startup states (running, verifying, recovering, merge_queue, and awaiting_input) (src/db/recovery.ts:46-53, src/db/recovery.ts:31-37). Depending on each item's state, checkpoint, runner status, and recovery history, Paws either resumes the item in a fresh session (or reattaches to an ongoing runner task), triggers a re-verification, leaves queued merges in place, skips items that are already parked or retrying, or posts a restart question in Linear (src/db/recovery.ts:57-88, src/core/recovery.ts:75-106).

Before processing work items, Paws shifts open runner leases by the duration of downtime (up to offlineBudgetMs) so downtime does not penalize active leases (src/db/recovery.ts:42-44, src/db/recovery.ts:51-52). It then inspects each item and applies startup logic:

1. Pre-decision checks and skips: If ensureRestartQuestion flags the item, Paws records an ask_restart decision (src/db/recovery.ts:58-61). If the item has a parked capacity wait (hasParkedCapacityWait), a pending answer resume (hasPendingAnswerResume), or a pending transient retry (hasPendingTransientRetry), Paws skips taking action because the next attempt is already accounted for (src/db/recovery.ts:62-64, src/db/recovery.ts:103-114).
2. Decision evaluation via decideStartup: For items evaluated by decideStartup, Paws checks item state and runtime conditions (src/db/recovery.ts:65-74, src/core/recovery.ts:84-92):
- Merge Queue: An item in merge_queue with no active run keeps its place (keep_place), noting whether a merge call was in flight (mergeCallInFlight) so GitHub can be queried first (src/db/recovery.ts:42-43, src/core/recovery.ts:78-80, src/core/recovery.ts:95-96). If its run was still active or a merge was already in progress, it triggers a reverify decision instead (src/core/recovery.ts:80-81, src/core/recovery.ts:94-97).
- Active Runner Work: If a paired runner still holds the work (runnerHoldsWork), an item in verifying state triggers reverify to attach to that Closeout review or check run (src/db/recovery.ts:75-82, src/core/recovery.ts:81-82, src/core/recovery.ts:98), while other states receive resume with freshSession: true and reattach: true (src/core/recovery.ts:99-100).
- Crash Loop Protection: If an item already has 1 or more recovery attempts and resumed less than RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS ago, Paws yields an ask_restart decision to ask in Linear rather than looping (src/core/recovery.ts:77-78, src/core/recovery.ts:101-102, src/core/recovery.test.ts:92-109).
- Verifying: An item in verifying with a candidate checkpoint commit re-verifies (reverify with resumed: true) (src/core/recovery.ts:103-104, src/core/recovery.ts:63-69).
- Default Resume: Otherwise, active items receive resume with freshSession: true from their checkpoint or branch (src/core/recovery.ts:76-77, src/core/recovery.ts:105).
3. Application and Staggering: Unless the item was already cut short mid-re-verify or mid-resume and reattaching to open work, Paws invokes applyDecision (src/db/recovery.ts:75-86). Resumed items are staggered by STARTUP_RESUME_SPACING_MS (5 seconds between items) (src/db/recovery.ts:55-56, src/db/recovery.ts:84-86, src/db/recovery.ts:39).

Finally, for any work items in awaiting_input, Paws releases their run capacity if they hold a run ID (src/db/recovery.ts:89-91). If any items remain awaiting input, Paws enqueues a catchup job to process open questions (src/db/recovery.ts:92-98).

q02fastGemini 3.8 Flashuseful6.4 sWhat happens when Paws restarts again while a task it already resumed once after a restart is still unfinished?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: ask_restart condition and precedence right; misses applyAskRestart effects, says so.

When Paws restarts while an unfinished task has already been resumed once (its recoveryAttempts is 1 or more) and less than RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS elapsed since that resume, startup recovery does not automatically resume it again; instead, it yields a { type: "ask_restart" } decision (src/core/recovery.ts:101-102). According to documentation comments in src/core/recovery.ts, this prompts in Linear whether to start the task again (src/core/recovery.ts:76-78).

During startup, recoverOnStartup in src/db/recovery.ts inspects items in startup states (src/db/recovery.ts:53). Before checking normal decision paths, if ensureRestartQuestion returns true, it immediately emits { type: "ask_restart" } (src/db/recovery.ts:58-61). It also skips items parked waiting for capacity, pending answer resumes, or pending transient retries (src/db/recovery.ts:62-64). Otherwise, it invokes decideStartup with the item's state, recoveryAttempts, checkpoint, and timing details such as sinceResumeMs (calculated as now - item.resumedAt) (src/db/recovery.ts:66-74).

Inside decideStartup in src/core/recovery.ts, special conditions take priority before the retry limit check: if the runner still holds active work, Paws either re-verifies or reattaches to the runner's session without asking (src/core/recovery.ts:98-100). Merge queue tasks and in-progress merges also follow their own paths (src/core/recovery.ts:95-97). But if those do not apply and recoveryAttempts >= 1 with sinceResumeMs < RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS, decideStartup returns { type: "ask_restart" } (src/core/recovery.ts:101-102), which recoverOnStartup records and applies (src/db/recovery.ts:84-87).

Caveats
  • Only 6 ranges across 4 files were inspected; the implementation details of `ensureRestartQuestion`, `applyDecision`, and the Linear notification mechanism were not included in the provided evidence.

decideStartup returns ask_restart when recoveryAttempts is at least 1 and less than RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS (30 minutes) passed since the resume. applyAskRestart fails the item with resume_already_attempted when it has no Linear session; otherwise it moves a running or verifying item to recovering, records a restart hold, cancels its open jobs, releases run capacity and enqueues the RESTART_QUESTION asking in Linear whether to start it again. Caveat: after 30 minutes a further restart resumes again instead of asking.

q02deepGemini 3.8 Flashuseful51.1 sWhat happens when Paws restarts again while a task it already resumed once after a restart is still unfinished?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: applyAskRestart steps incl. no-session failure and question text; window value marked unseen.

When Paws restarts while a task is still unfinished after having already been resumed once from a restart, Paws refuses to resume the task automatically and instead places it on hold to ask in Linear whether it should be started again (src/core/recovery.ts:76-78, src/core/recovery.ts:101-102, src/db/decisions.ts:91, src/db/restart-hold.ts:5-6).

During startup recovery, recoverOnStartup in src/db/recovery.ts iterates through in-flight items (src/db/recovery.ts:53, src/db/recovery.ts:57). If an active restart question hold already exists via ensureRestartQuestion, it pushes an ask_restart decision immediately (src/db/recovery.ts:58-61). Otherwise, unless blocked by a capacity wait, pending answer resume, or transient retry, it calls decideStartup with the item's state, checkpoint, and recoveryAttempts count (src/db/recovery.ts:62-74).

Inside decideStartup in src/core/recovery.ts, if the runner does not still hold active work and the merge queue or reverification conditions do not apply, it checks whether input.recoveryAttempts >= 1 and whether the time elapsed since the previous resume is within RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS (src/core/recovery.ts:98-102). If both criteria match, decideStartup returns { type: "ask_restart" } (src/core/recovery.ts:101-102).

When applyDecision receives ask_restart, it invokes applyAskRestart in src/db/decisions.ts (src/db/decisions.ts:40-42, src/db/decisions.ts:91-111):
1. If the item has no associated sessionKey, it marks the item as failed via failWorkItem with reason "resume_already_attempted" and the message *"Stopped after a restart because this run was already resumed once."* (src/db/decisions.ts:93-101).
2. If the item is in running or verifying, an event lease_expired is applied (src/db/decisions.ts:103-104).
3. It records a restart hold on the item via holdRestart in src/db/restart-hold.ts (src/db/decisions.ts:106, src/db/restart-hold.ts:23-30).
4. If a restart question is not already open, it cancels all open jobs for the item (reason: "restart_question"), releases any allocated run capacity, and calls ensureRestartQuestion (src/db/decisions.ts:107-110).
5. ensureRestartQuestion queues an item.ask job containing the prompt: *"Paws restarted twice while this task was running. Start it again from its branch in a fresh session? Stop the session to leave it."* with an option to "Start again" (src/db/restart-hold.ts:5-6, src/db/restart-hold.ts:55-71).

Caveats

Expected (reviewer key)

decideStartup returns ask_restart when recoveryAttempts is at least 1 and less than RESUME_AGAIN_AFTER_MS (30 minutes) passed since the resume. applyAskRestart fails the item with resume_already_attempted when it has no Linear session; otherwise it moves a running or verifying item to recovering, records a restart hold, cancels its open jobs, releases run capacity and enqueues the RESTART_QUESTION asking in Linear whether to start it again. Caveat: after 30 minutes a further restart resumes again instead of asking.

q03fastGemini 3.8 Flashuseful7.5 sWhat does Paws do to running work items when it shuts down on SIGTERM?

Review: prepareShutdown sequence correct.

When Paws handles SIGTERM, it triggers shutdown via shutdownPaws (src/index.ts:2054-2061), which uses prepareShutdown to commit in-flight work and transition running work items (src/db/recovery.ts:165-177, test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:249-261). First, if a commit callback is supplied, it commits work-in-progress (WIP) on each in-flight item branch, catching and journaling errors so missing worktrees do not block shutdown (src/db/recovery.ts:178-186, test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:257-259).

Next, inside an immediate database transaction, it updates the liveness timestamp with markPawsAlive and evaluates all items in running or verifying states (src/db/recovery.ts:188-191). If an item has a parked capacity wait or if a runner still holds the work (such as an active agent turn, Closeout review, or check run), it is skipped and retains its state (src/db/recovery.ts:167-169, src/db/recovery.ts:192, src/db/recovery.ts:208-214). Otherwise, if the item has an associated currentRunId, that run is marked as lost (src/db/recovery.ts:193). If the item does not satisfy keepsVerification, Paws applies a lease_expired event to it, moving the item into the recovering state (src/db/recovery.ts:166-167, src/db/recovery.ts:194, test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:260-261).

Items in the merge_queue state are also inspected: if their run is currently active, that run is marked as lost and a lease_expired event is applied to the item; otherwise, waiting merge queue items retain their state and position for subsequent startup (src/db/recovery.ts:169-171, src/db/recovery.ts:196-200, src/db/recovery.ts:204-206).

Expected (reviewer key)

The shutdown flush calls prepareShutdown with a callback that commits dirty files on each in-flight item's worktree as 'wip: shutdown' when the item has a run commit policy; a failed commit is journaled and does not stop shutdown. Then, in one transaction, it marks Paws alive and, for running and verifying items that are not parked on capacity and not held by a runner, marks the run lost and moves the item to recovering unless it is verifying with a candidate. Merge-queue items keep their place unless their run is still active. This does not spend the one resume attempt.

q03deepGemini 3.8 Flashuseful20.3 sWhat does Paws do to running work items when it shuts down on SIGTERM?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Adds commit policy and wiring in src/index.ts.

When Paws receives SIGTERM, it triggers shutdownPaws, which executes its shutdown stages and flushes durable database state via prepareShutdown (src/index.ts:2055-2061, src/shutdown.ts:61-68, src/index.ts:1545-1577).

For running work items, Paws carries out the following steps:

1. Commits work-in-progress (WIP): For each in-flight item, Paws retrieves its commit policy via getItemRunCommitPolicy and synchronously commits dirty working tree files with the message "wip: shutdown" (src/db/recovery.ts:178-186, src/index.ts:1568-1577). If committing fails, the error is journaled and shutdown continues without aborting the lease move (src/db/recovery.ts:182-184).
2. Records liveliness: Inside an immediate transaction, Paws updates its heartbeat via markPawsAlive (src/db/recovery.ts:188-189).
3. Updates items in running and verifying states:
- It checks whether an item is waiting on capacity (hasParkedCapacityWait) or if a remote runner still holds the work lease (runnerHoldsWork) (src/db/recovery.ts:190-192). If either is true, the item is skipped and keeps its current state (src/db/recovery.ts:167-169, src/db/recovery.ts:192).
- Otherwise, if the item has a current run (item.currentRunId!== null), that run is marked as "lost" (src/db/recovery.ts:193).
- Unless the item keeps verification (keepsVerification(item)), Paws emits a lease_expired work item event (src/db/recovery.ts:194), which transitions running work items to the "recovering" state without consuming a resume attempt (src/db/recovery.ts:166-167, test/shutdown-wip.test.ts:260-261).
4. Updates active runs in the merge queue: For items in merge_queue whose run is still active (runActive), the current run is marked as "lost" and a lease_expired event is applied (src/db/recovery.ts:196-200). An item waiting in the merge queue without an active run retains its state and position (src/db/recovery.ts:169-171, src/db/recovery.ts:196-197).

q04fastGemini 3.8 Flashuseful14.5 sHow does a Linear webhook delivery become work for the orchestrator?
2/2 correct1/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome partial

Review: Handler pipeline right; says the orchestrator hand-off is not covered.

A Linear webhook delivery becomes work by being verified, parsed into an accepted event, committed to an inbox store, and then dispatched asynchronously through an intake queue or event handler (src/linear/webhook.ts:107-153).

When a request arrives at handleLinearWebhook, the handler performs the following sequence:
1. It validates the request headers and payload, checking for a valid 64-character hex Linear-Signature, verifying the HMAC-SHA256 signature against the raw request body using checkLinearHmac, and ensuring the timestamp (from the body's webhookTimestamp or the linear-timestamp header) is within a 60-second window via checkLinearTimestamp (src/linear/webhook.ts:17, src/linear/webhook.ts:63-72, src/linear/webhook.ts:112-138, src/linear/webhook.ts:182-196).
2. It verifies the presence of the linear-delivery header and parses the payload using parseAgentEvent to produce an AcceptedLinearEvent containing session IDs, issue IDs, activity details, deduplication keys, and action/signal classifications (src/linear/webhook.ts:131-141, src/linear/webhook.ts:198-255).
3. It updates the webhook sync cursor (linear:webhook) in the configured InboxStore and commits the event via deps.store.commit(event) to persist and deduplicate it (src/linear/webhook.ts:49-50, src/linear/webhook.ts:142-147).
4. It hands off the event without blocking the HTTP response: if an IntakeQueue is configured and accepts the event (created or prompted events), the handler calls deps.intake.arrive(event) for newly inserted events or deps.intake.wake() if already existing but unhandled (src/linear/webhook.ts:42-43, src/linear/webhook.ts:103-106, src/linear/webhook.ts:148-150). For events not accepted by the intake queue that are inserted or unhandled, it calls schedule, which invokes deps.onEvent in a background promise and marks the event handled in the store upon completion (src/linear/webhook.ts:151-171).

The webhook endpoint immediately returns a 200 JSON response ({ ok: true, duplicate:... }) so it stays within Linear's 5-second acknowledgment budget (src/linear/webhook.ts:103-106, src/linear/webhook.ts:152). How the intake queue or onEvent callback specifically translates the event into database work items or orchestrator jobs is not covered in the inspected files (src/linear/webhook.ts:39-45, src/linear/webhook.ts:148-171).

This is based on 6 source ranges in 4 files, not the whole repository. Asking again with mode "deep" can follow the remaining leads.

Caveats
  • The implementation of `IntakeQueue`, `InboxStore`, and the orchestrator's `onEvent` callback were not included in the provided evidence, so the exact steps where intake creates orchestrator jobs or work items cannot be shown.

Expected (reviewer key)

The server routes POST /webhooks/linear to handleLinearWebhook when webhooks are enabled. The handler checks the HMAC signature and a 60 second timestamp window, requires a delivery id, parses the agent event, records it durably in the inbox store and answers 200 without waiting. Created and prompted events go to the intake queue, which posts the first activity on arrival and runs at most two intakes at once, oldest first, keeping each session in order. Each intake calls followUp, which hands the event to orchestrator.onLinearEvent and then reconciles the linked work item.

q04deepGemini 3.8 Flashuseful30.0 sHow does a Linear webhook delivery become work for the orchestrator?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: Reaches followUp -> orchestrator.onLinearEvent and reconcile, matching the key.

A Linear webhook delivery becomes work for the orchestrator by passing HMAC and timestamp verification, being parsed into an AcceptedLinearEvent, committing to an inbox store for deduplication, and flowing via either an intake queue or direct event scheduling to a followUp callback that calls orchestrator.onLinearEvent(event) (src/linear/webhook.ts:102-153, src/linear/webhook.ts:198-255, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:253-258, src/index.ts:428-430).

When an incoming HTTP POST hits handleLinearWebhook, the system checks the linear-signature and linear-delivery headers, enforces that the secret is set, and reads the raw body with readWebhookBody up to 1 MB within 5 seconds (src/linear/webhook.ts:112-125, src/webhook-body/index.ts:7-8). It validates the HMAC-SHA256 signature and confirms that the timestamp in the payload or linear-timestamp header falls within a 60-second window (TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_MS) (src/linear/webhook.ts:17, src/linear/webhook.ts:67-72, src/linear/webhook.ts:126-138). If any check fails, the rejection is recorded in failure tracking and returned with status 400 or 401 (src/linear/webhook.ts:117-138, src/linear/webhook.ts:173-180). If verification succeeds, the webhook cursor timestamp linear:webhook is updated in the store, and verification failure counts for the store are cleared (src/linear/webhook.ts:145-146).

parseAgentEvent then transforms the raw JSON payload into an AcceptedLinearEvent (src/linear/webhook.ts:140, src/linear/webhook.ts:198-254). It inspects fields such as agentSession and agentActivity, extracts sessionId, issueId, and activityId, determines whether the event represents a session closure, a stop signal, or an action like created or prompted, and computes a deterministic dedupeKey (src/linear/webhook.ts:211-254).

The parsed event is committed to the inbox store via deps.store.commit(event) (src/linear/webhook.ts:147). Delivery to the orchestrator then branches depending on intake configuration (src/linear/webhook.ts:148-151):

1. If an intake queue is present and accepts the event (created and prompted events), new events invoke deps.intake.arrive(event), while unhandled duplicates invoke deps.intake.wake() (src/linear/webhook.ts:42-43, src/linear/webhook.ts:148-150). In createLinearIntake, arrival triggers immediate session acknowledgement, while the queue's worker acknowledges the session and delegates to the configured followUp callback wrapped in linearCaller("intake",...) (src/linear/webhook.ts:103-105, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:245-258).
2. If the intake queue does not accept the event, unhandled events are scheduled through schedule(deps, event), which records the event dedupe key in an in-flight set, invokes deps.onEvent(event), marks it handled in the store, and catches errors into the journal (src/linear/webhook.ts:151-170).

In src/index.ts, openLinear wires this intake pipeline to the system orchestrator: followUp invokes await orchestrator.onLinearEvent(event) (src/linear/runtime.ts:109-122, src/index.ts:428-430, src/index.ts:594). If the orchestrator accepts the event, existing intake reads are retrieved, and if a session is linked to an active work item in a workspace, it triggers reconciler.reconcile (src/index.ts:430-442). Additionally, stop commands handled via submitCommand persist into the database job table under JOB_KIND.command for execution (src/linear/runtime.ts:71-72, src/linear/poller.ts:416-429).

q05fastGemini 3.8 Flashuseful6.2 sHow does a person's bypass of a failed Closeout check reach the Closeout decision?
2/2 correct1/2 useful2/2 clear1/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: applyBypasses matching and outcome correct; does not show recoveryOptions; outcome 'supported' is generous.

A person bypasses a failed Closeout check by providing their Linear user ID, their name, and a reason for the bypass against a specific ask question and evaluated head (src/closeout/bypass.ts:3-15, src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:3-20). These recorded bypass approvals reach the gate via CloseoutGateOptions.bypasses and are evaluated against the current run using applyBypasses (src/closeout/gate.ts:55, src/closeout/bypass.ts:21-24).

Inside applyBypasses, each bypass approval is filtered and accepted only if its metadata matches the decision context: the bypass's taskId, base, head, and policyDigest must equal the decision's candidate task, base SHA, head SHA, and policy digest, and both the actor and reason strings must not be blank (src/closeout/bypass.ts:27-35). In addition, all IDs in checkIds must correspond to decision items whose state is either bypassable (failed, exhausted, or independence), passed, or skipped (src/closeout/bypass.ts:17-19, src/closeout/bypass.ts:35-42).

If valid matching bypasses are found, their checkIds are collected into a set, and applyBypasses recalculates the remaining non-passed, non-skipped items (excluding setup failures) after filtering out those bypassed IDs (src/closeout/bypass.ts:44-51). The final evaluation outcome is then updated: it resolves to accepted if no failed items remain, exhausted if any remaining item is exhausted, rejected if every remaining item is failed, or blocked otherwise, attaching the applied bypasses to the evaluation (src/closeout/bypass.ts:52-60).

Expected (reviewer key)

A bypass is approved on the item page, not by a Linear reply. recoveryOptions reads the item's Closeout recoveries and, for link asks decided 'approve', turns each approved check with a reason into a CloseoutBypass carrying task, base, head and policy digest. The orchestrator spreads recoveryOptions into the Closeout gate options, and evaluateCandidate applies applyBypasses to the native evaluation. A bypass only counts when task, base, head and policy digest match exactly and the check is bypassable; the outcome becomes accepted only when nothing else remains, and the summary lists who approved each bypass.

When Closeout stops on failed checks, a human bypass recorded through a link question flows into the orchestrator loop, is passed into Closeout gate options, and is applied directly to the gate evaluation outcome (src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:14-54, src/closeout/run.ts:529-532, src/loop/closeout-help.ts:56-98, src/closeout/run.ts:144).

1. Capturing and storing the bypass: When Closeout stops with failed checks on a candidate, askCloseoutHelp generates a link question (kind: "bypass" or "rule") and saves the failed checks via saveCloseoutBypassChecks (src/loop/closeout-help.ts:56-98). In the UI, the person selects failed checks and enters a reason on the bypass card (src/web/src/client/link-ask.ts:145-168). When submitted with an approval, the check row in SQLite records approvedBy, approvedByName, and reason (src/db/closeout-bypass.ts:15-20, src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:37-51).
2. Loading recoveries for the candidate run: When assembling options for an evaluation or decision, recoveryOptions queries listCloseoutRecoveries and checks the link question decision (src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:14-37). If the decision is approve, it reads the approved checks using listCloseoutBypassChecks and constructs CloseoutBypass objects matching the recovery's taskId, base, head, and policyDigest, including checkIds: [check.checkId], actor: check.approvedBy, and reason: check.reason (src/loop/closeout-recovery.ts:37-52).
3. Supplying bypasses to the gate: These bypasses are provided in GateInput.bypasses or CloseoutGateOptions.bypasses when invoking Closeout evaluation (evaluateCandidate) or re-deciding existing evidence (decideCloseoutGate via decideRecorded) (src/closeout/gate.ts:55, src/closeout/run.ts:484-532, src/closeout/run.ts:110, src/closeout/run.ts:128-144).
4. Filtering and applying in applyBypasses: applyBypasses verifies that the candidate evaluation is not invalid, has a valid policy digest, and matches the bypass's taskId, base, head, and policyDigest (src/closeout/bypass.ts:25-32). It also verifies that actor and reason are non-empty and that every bypassed check exists on the decision in a bypassable state (failed, exhausted, or independence), or is already passed or skipped (src/closeout/bypass.ts:17-19, src/closeout/bypass.ts:33-42).
5. Computing the final decision: applyBypasses removes the bypassed check IDs from the unsatisfied items (src/closeout/bypass.ts:45-51). If no unsatisfied items remain, the outcome becomes accepted; otherwise, depending on the remaining items, it becomes exhausted, rejected, or blocked (src/closeout/bypass.ts:52-60). Finally, finalResult attaches the accepted bypasses to GateResult.bypasses and writes bypassSummary into the summary text (specifying the check ID, reason, actor, head, policy digest, and question ID) (src/closeout/bypass.ts:64-74, src/closeout/run.ts:1245-1285).

q07fastGemini 3.8 Flashuseful7.9 sWhat happens when a Linear intake fails, and how is it retried?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: All three error paths, ladder, pump timer, lane ordering.

When a Linear intake delivery encounters an error in createIntakeQueue, the error is first logged to the journal via journalCaught (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-109). What happens next depends on the type of error:

1. Deleted session: If the error is a LinearEntityNotFoundError for an AgentSession, the queue logs that the session no longer exists, marks the event as handled via store.markHandled(event.dedupeKey), and does not retry (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:111-114).
2. Rate limits: If the error is a LinearRateLimitError, the queue updates its global hold timestamp pausedUntil to at least now + error.retryAfterMs (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:118-119). It records the failure in the store using store.markFailed(event.dedupeKey, { error: message, nextAttemptAt: at + Math.max(error.retryAfterMs, INTAKE_RETRY_MS[0]), counted: false }), which delays the retry without incrementing the attempt count (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:120-125).
3. Other intake failures: For standard errors, the attempt counter is incremented (queued.attempts + 1) and the retry backoff is computed using intakeRetryMs(attempts) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:127-128). The failure is recorded in the store with store.markFailed(event.dedupeKey, { error: message, nextAttemptAt: at + waitMs, counted: true }) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:129-133).

Retries are driven by the queue's pump() mechanism (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:140, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:73-100). Failed events wait out their scheduled nextAttemptAt without blocking unrelated events, while preserving per-session or per-issue ordering (event.sessionId?? event.issueId) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:37-40, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:83-86, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:87-89). Standard retries back off using INTAKE_RETRY_MS, which defines delays of 30 seconds, 1 minute, 2 minutes, 5 minutes, and 10 minutes (holding at 10 minutes for any subsequent attempts) (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:12-19). When pump() encounters an event whose nextAttemptAt is still in the future, it arms a timer for the remaining duration (next - at) to wake the queue and retry once the delay elapses (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:87-89, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:99).

This is based on 6 source ranges in 4 files, not the whole repository. Asking again with mode "deep" can follow the remaining leads.

Caveats
  • Based on 6 inspected source ranges in 4 files at commit 2ac93023d31b; the rest of the repository was not read for this answer.
Expected (reviewer key)

The intake worker catches the error and journals it. A missing AgentSession is marked handled and skipped. A Linear rate limit pauses the whole queue for its retry-after and reschedules the event without counting an attempt, waiting at least 30 seconds. Any other failure counts an attempt and reschedules that event after 30 s, 1 min, 2 min, 5 min, then every 10 min, without blocking other events, and logs the retry. Nothing is retried after the queue is stopped.

q07deepGemini 3.8 Flashuseful21.3 sWhat happens when a Linear intake fails, and how is it retried?
2/2 correct2/2 useful2/2 clear2/2 uncertainty2/2 citationsoutcome supported

Review: As fast plus concurrency 2 and first-attempt-only failure activity.

When a queued Linear intake delivery fails, the error is caught, logged to the journal, and classified to determine whether the event should be dropped or recorded as failed with a scheduled retry time (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:108-137). If the error indicates that the session no longer exists (LinearEntityNotFoundError for AgentSession), the event is skipped and marked handled in the inbox store (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:111-115). If the failure is due to a LinearRateLimitError, the queue pauses future runs until the rate limit expires, and records the failure in the database with counted: false so that it does not consume a retry attempt; its nextAttemptAt is set to at least INTAKE_RETRY_MS[0] (30 seconds) or the error's retryAfterMs (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:118-125). For all other errors, the attempt count is incremented, and store.markFailed records the truncated error message, the incremented attempt count, and a new nextAttemptAt timestamp (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:127-133, src/linear/inbox.ts:123-130).

Retries are driven by createIntakeQueue using a backoff schedule defined in INTAKE_RETRY_MS: 30 seconds for the 1st failed attempt, 60 seconds for the 2nd, 120 seconds (2 minutes) for the 3rd, 300 seconds (5 minutes) for the 4th, and 600 seconds (10 minutes) for the 5th and any subsequent attempts (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:12-19, test/linear-intake-queue.test.ts:226-227). Whenever a task finishes or the queue wakes via pump(), the queue inspects pending events in inbox_event via store.listQueued() (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:140, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:73-81, src/linear/inbox.ts:104-122). It skips events whose nextAttemptAt timestamp is in the future and sets an unreferenced timer for the earliest pending retry time (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:61-71, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:87-89, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:99). Once the timestamp is reached, the worker picks up the event in order—ensuring per-session or per-issue ordering and respecting a concurrency cap of 2—and invokes deliver again with the updated attempt count (src/linear/intake-queue.ts:9-10, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:79-107, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:287).

On the user-facing side, if the failure occurred while running through acknowledgeNewSession, terminal non-transient errors report an error activity back to Linear on the initial attempt, but set reportFailure: false on retries (mode.attempts > 0) so duplicate failure activities are not posted to Linear across every retry attempt (src/linear/acknowledge.ts:62-63, src/linear/acknowledge.ts:134-157, src/linear/intake-queue.ts:263).
